en: Points of Controversy:
The Chapter on Latent Tendencies,
Eleventh Section.
The Discussion on the Seven Underlying Tendencies:
Are the underlying tendencies indeterminate? Yes.
Is resultant-indeterminate, functional-indeterminate, matter, Nibbāna, the eye-base …pe… and the tangible-base indeterminate?
One should not say so …pe….
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust indeterminate?
“Yes,” you say.
“Then is sensual lust, the obsession of sensual lust, the fetter of sensual lust, the flood of sensual desire, the yoke of sensual desire, and the hindrance of sensual desire indeterminate?
You should not speak thus … [as before] …
Is sensual lust, the obsession of sensual lust, and so forth, up to the hindrance of sensual desire unwholesome?
Yes. Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust unwholesome?
It should not be said thus...
[as before] ...Is the underlying tendency to aversion indeterminate? Yes.
Is aversion, the obsession of aversion, and the fetter of aversion indeterminate?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is aversion,
the obsession of aversion, and the fetter of aversion unwholesome?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is the underlying tendency to aversion unwholesome?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is the underlying tendency to conceit indeterminate? Yes.
Is conceit, the obsession of conceit, and the fetter of conceit indeterminate?
It should not be said thus ... [as before] ...
Is conceit, the obsession of conceit, the fetter of conceit, unwholesome? Yes.
Is the underlying tendency to conceit unwholesome?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is the underlying tendency to views indeterminate?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Then is view, the flood of views, the yoke of views, the obsession of views, and the fetter of views indeterminate?
You should not speak thus …pe…
Is view, the flood of views, the yoke of views, the obsession of views, and the fetter of views unwholesome?
Yes. Is the underlying tendency to views unwholesome?
It should not be stated thus … [as before] … Is the underlying tendency to doubt indeterminate? Yes.
Is doubt, the obsession of doubt, the fetter of doubt, and the hindrance of doubt indeterminate?
One should not say so… Is doubt,
the obsession of doubt, the fetter of doubt, and the hindrance of doubt unwholesome?
“Yes.
“Is the underlying tendency to doubt unwholesome?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is the underlying tendency to lust for existence indeterminate?
Yes. Is lust for existence, the obsession of lust for existence, and the fetter of lust for existence indeterminate? Yes.
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is lust for existence,
the obsession of lust for existence, and the fetter of lust for existence unwholesome? Yes.
Is the underlying tendency to lust for existence unwholesome?
One should not say so … [as before] … Is the underlying tendency to ignorance indeterminate?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is ignorance (avijjā), the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance, indeterminate (abyākata)?
You should not speak thus … [and so on] …
Is ignorance (avijjā), the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance unwholesome?
Yes. Is the underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) unwholesome?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Should it not be said that “the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are indeterminate (abyākata)”?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “When a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring in an ordinary person (puthujjana), should he be called ‘one who possesses latent tendencies’?
“Yes.”
“Are wholesome and unwholesome states present before one?
“One should not say so.
… [as before] … “Therefore, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are indeterminate (abyākata).”
Is it to be said that an ordinary person (puthujjana) is "with lust" when a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring?
Yes. Do wholesome and unwholesome states come into manifestation? Yes.
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Therefore, lust is indeterminate.
Are the underlying tendencies rootless?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is form (rūpa) nibbāna, the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), and so on, up to the tangible-object-base (phoṭṭhabbāyatana)?
You should not speak thus … and so forth.
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust rootless?
Yes. Is sensual lust, the obsession by sensual lust, the fetter of sensual lust, and the hindrance of sensual desire rootless? [Yes.]
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is sensual lust,
the obsession of sensual lust … pe … the hindrance of sensual desire caused by a cause? Yes.
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust accompanied by a cause?
One should not say so …pe… [and so on for] the underlying tendency to aversion …pe…
the underlying tendency to conceit … the underlying tendency to views … the underlying tendency to doubt …
Is the underlying tendency to lust for existence … the underlying tendency to ignorance causeless? Yes.
Is ignorance (avijjā) the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, the obsession of ignorance, the fetter of ignorance, the hindrance of ignorance, and causeless?
One should not say so...
[and so on] ...ignorance is the flood of ignorance... [and so on].
Is the hindrance of ignorance accompanied by a cause?
Yes. Is the underlying tendency of ignorance accompanied by a cause?
It should not be said thus ...
[as before] ... Should it not be said that “the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are rootless”?
Agreed.
When a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring in an ordinary person (puthujjana), should he be called "one who possesses latent tendencies" (sānusaya)?
Agreed.
Are the underlying tendencies (anusaya) "with cause" by virtue of that reason?
One should not say so...
[and so forth] ...therefore, the underlying tendencies are "without cause."
Is an ordinary person (puthujjana) to be called "one possessed of lust" when a wholesome or indeterminate state of consciousness is occurring?
Yes. Is lust, by that reason, accompanied by a root (sahetuka)?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Therefore, lust is without cause.
Are the underlying tendencies dissociated from consciousness?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is form, Nibbāna, the eye-base … [and so on] … the tangible-object-base?
You should not speak thus … [as before].
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust dissociated from the mind? Yes.
Is sensual lust, the obsession of sensual lust, the fetter of sensual lust, the flood of sensuality, the yoke of sensuality, and the hindrance of sensual desire dissociated from the mind? [No.]
It should not be said thus … [and so on] … Is sensual lust,
the obsession of sensual lust … the hindrance of sensual desire associated with consciousness? Yes.
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust associated with consciousness?
One should not say so … [and so on] … Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust dissociated from consciousness?
“Yes.
“To which aggregate does it belong?
“It belongs to the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha).”
Is the aggregate of volitional formations dissociated from mind?
One should not say so.
Is the aggregate of volitional formations dissociated from mind? One should not say so.
“Yes.
[If you say this,] should it not be said that the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception are dissociated from consciousness?
You should not speak thus … [and so on].
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust included within the aggregate of formations and dissociated from the mind?
Yes. Is sensual lust included within the aggregate of formations and dissociated from the mind?
It should not be said so … [as before] … Is sensual lust included within the aggregate of mental formations and associated with consciousness? Yes.
Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust included in the aggregate of mental formations and associated with consciousness?
One should not say so… [etc.

… Is the underlying tendency to sensual lust included in the aggregate of mental formations and dissociated from consciousness, while sensual lust itself is included in the aggregate of mental formations and associated with consciousness?
“Yes,” [you say].

“Then is it to be said that one part of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is associated with consciousness (cittasampayutta) and one part is dissociated from consciousness (cittavippayutta)?
You should not say so … [and so on] …
Is one part of the aggregate of mental formations associated with consciousness and one part dissociated from consciousness? Yes.
Is one part of the aggregate of feeling and one part of the aggregate of perception associated with consciousness and one part dissociated from consciousness?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is the underlying tendency to aversion,

the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance dissociated from consciousness? Yes.
Is ignorance (avijjā), the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance dissociated from consciousness?
One should not say so... [and so on] ...
Is ignorance, the flood of ignorance, the yoke of ignorance, and the hindrance of ignorance associated with consciousness?
“Yes.
“Then is the underlying tendency to ignorance associated with consciousness?
“One should not say so,” and so forth.
Is the underlying tendency to ignorance dissociated from consciousness?
Yes. To which aggregate does it belong?
"It is included within the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). "Is the aggregate of mental formations dissociated from consciousness?
One should not say so.
Is the aggregate of mental formations dissociated from consciousness? Yes.
Are the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception dissociated from consciousness?
It should not be said thus … [as before] … Is the underlying tendency to ignorance included in the aggregate of formations and dissociated from consciousness? Yes.
Is ignorance included within the aggregate of volitional formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*) and dissociated from mind (*cittavippayutta*)?
One should not say so …pe… Is ignorance included within the aggregate of volitional formations and associated with mind (*cittasampayutta*)?
“Yes,” [you say].
“Is the underlying tendency to ignorance included within the aggregate of volitional formations and associated with consciousness?
One should not speak thus … [and so on] …

The underlying tendency to ignorance (avijjānusaya) is included within the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and is dissociated from consciousness (cittavippayutta); whereas ignorance and the aggregate of formations are included [within that same aggregate] and are associated with consciousness (cittasampayutta)?
Yes. Is it then the case that one part of the aggregate of formations is associated with consciousness and another part is dissociated from consciousness?
It should not be said thus.
Is it the case that one part of the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is associated with consciousness and another part is dissociated from consciousness?
Yes, it is.
Is the aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception partly associated with consciousness and partly dissociated from consciousness?
It should not be stated thus… [and so on]… It should not be stated.
“Are the underlying tendencies dissociated from consciousness?”—
Yes. “When a wholesome or indeterminate consciousness is occurring in an ordinary person, should he be said to be ‘possessed of underlying tendencies’?”— Yes.
“Yes,” [you say].
“Are the underlying tendencies associated with that consciousness?
You should not say so.
In that case, the underlying tendencies (anusaya) are dissociated from consciousness.
Is it then to be said that an ordinary person (puthujjana), while a wholesome or neutral state of consciousness is occurring, is "possessed of lust" (sarāga)?
Yes, it is.
Is lust associated with that consciousness?
One should not say so.
Therefore, lust is dissociated from consciousness.
The discussion on the three underlying tendencies is finished.
